title: Study examines lifetime fluoride exposure and cognition in older Irish adults
html:
Dental Tribune International

Tue. 24. November 2026

share save

DUBLIN, Ireland: Although community water fluoridation has well-established benefits for oral health, concerns about its potential effects on neurological development have fuelled growing public debate. Previous research has largely focused on fluoride exposure during early life, leaving questions about the potential cognitive effects of exposure across the lifespan. A recent study has investigated the association between lifetime exposure to fluoridated drinking water and cognitive performance in older Irish adults and examined whether this association differed according to exposure during early life. The findings provide further evidence to inform the ongoing debate about the long-term cognitive safety of community water fluoridation.

Co-author Dr Lina Zgaga, professor in epidemiology at Trinity College Dublin, commented in a university press release: “Ireland is unusual because it has a national policy of community water fluoridation. This creates an opportunity to do high-quality research in large studies and answer many outstanding questions around fluoridation.”

The researchers used data from the Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing, a nationally representative cohort study of adults aged 50 years and older, to estimate participants’ lifetime exposure to fluoridated drinking water over a period of at least 50 years. Most participants had been exposed to fluoridated drinking water for between one-quarter and three-quarters of their lives, and fewer than one in ten had been exposed for longer.

Although participants with high lifetime exposure showed better cognitive scores than those with low exposure, these differences were no longer statistically significant after taking socio-demographic, lifestyle and health-related factors into account. Overall, the researchers found no association between lifetime exposure to fluoridated drinking water and cognitive performance. They also found no statistically significant evidence that the findings differed according to whether participants had been exposed to fluoridated drinking water during the first five years of life. However, relatively few participants had been exposed during this period, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about the role of early-life exposure. Similarly, a US study examining childhood exposure to fluoride in drinking water and cognition across the life-course found no evidence of cognitive harm in adolescence or at 60 years of age among individuals exposed to recommended fluoridation concentrations.

“Our findings provide reassurance that lifetime exposure to fluoridated drinking water at the levels used in Ireland is not associated with poorer cognitive function in older adults,” said lead author Dr Vinay Sharma, a researcher at Trinity College Dublin’s School of Medicine.

The researchers hope that the findings will contribute to an evidence-based conversation about the safety of the community water fluoridation programme. Prof. Zgaga commented: “Having good, contemporary evidence is essential to support informed decisions about this public health intervention nationally and internationally and to ensure that policy continues to be based on the best available evidence.”

The researchers concluded that their findings, considered alongside the established oral health benefits of community water fluoridation, support the continued use of community water fluoridation. “Nonetheless, we should continue to check for any adverse effects of water fluoridation in the Irish population on an ongoing basis. This research establishes a way to monitor the health of water consumers, but should just be the baseline for future studies,” noted co-author Dr Brian O’Connell, professor of restorative dentistry at Trinity College Dublin.

The study, titled “Lifetime fluoride exposure and cognition in older Irish adults”, was published online on 4 November 2026 in the Journal of Dental Research, ahead of final publication.
